title: You’ve Got This
author: John McLean
summary: In Issue #29 of Dad's Lighthouse, the author remembers his father patiently teaching him to tie his shoes in 1964, then describes sixty years later sitting beside that same father, who had developed cognitive difficulties, and teaching him to use a TV remote and microwave. From both experiences he draws the week's tenet, care compassionately, which sometimes means letting a child struggle instead of fixing the problem. He quotes Wayne Dyer and Lao Tzu to argue that caring and controlling can look alike and that compassion takes courage. The practical exercise is to pause before helping, ask what the child thinks he should do, let him make low-stakes mistakes, and say only 'Nice work' when he succeeds. The piece closes with the lighthouse image of a father as a steady guide who does not steer the ship.
points: Real patience in teaching a skill, as his father showed with shoelaces, models care and is remembered long after the skill itself.
Protecting a child from every struggle makes childhood easier but does not make adulthood better, so protection and preparation should not be confused.
Caring and controlling can look remarkably similar, and a father's job is to help children become themselves, not smaller copies of him.
Pause before helping and ask 'What do you think you should do?', 'What have you tried?' or 'What are your options?'
When the child succeeds, avoid 'I told you so' and simply say 'Nice work', letting him own the moment.
quotes: And when I reflect on our shoe tying lessons, I realize the real lesson wasn’t how to tie a shoe. It was how to care about someone enough to patiently work with them through their challenges without getting frustrated or giving up.
But sometimes caring for someone means doing something much harder; it means letting them struggle.

I think there’s a lot of wisdom packed into that idea, because caring and controlling can look remarkably similar, and if we’re not careful, we start making decisions for someone simply because we believe we know what’s best for them.
But our job isn’t to create little versions of ourselves; it’s to help our kids become capable of becoming themselves.
Protecting a child from every struggle may make childhood easier, but it won’t make adulthood better.
You may be surprised by what happens when you don’t immediately provide the answer. Sometimes they’ll make a mistake. Let them do that a lot when the stakes are low.
The lighthouse doesn’t steer the ship, it stands there: Strong. Steady. Visible. Dependable.
